text:
She goes to the washbasin and washes her face and hands.

There! Give me a towel!—oh—the sun is rising!

JEAN

And then the troll bursts!

MISS

Yes, it is the trolls who have been abroad tonight!—But Jean, listen! Come with me, for now I have the means!

JEAN

hesitating.

Enough?

MISS

Enough to begin with! Come with me, for I cannot travel alone today. Just think, Midsummer Day, on a stifling train, packed in among crowds of people who will gape at one; standing still at the stations when one wanted to fly—no, I cannot, I cannot! And then the memories come; childhood memories of Midsummer Days, with the church decked in greenery—the birch leaves and lilacs; dinner with the table laid, the relatives, the friends; the afternoon in the park, dancing, music, flowers, and games! Oh, one flees, flees, but the memories follow in the baggage van, and remorse and pangs of conscience!

JEAN

I shall go with you! But now, at once, before it is too late! This very moment!

MISS

There! Get dressed, then!

Takes the birdcage.

JEAN

But no luggage! Then we shall be discovered!

MISS

No, nothing! Only what one can take in the compartment!

JEAN

has taken his hat.

What sort of thing have you there? What is it?

MISS

It is only my greenfinch! I do not want to leave it!

JEAN

Well, there we are! Are we to bring a birdcage now too! You are out of your mind! Put down the cage!

MISS

The only thing I am taking with me from home; the only living creature that is fond of me, since Diana was unfaithful to me! Do not be cruel! Let me take it with me!

JEAN

Put down the cage, I say—and do not speak so loudly—Kristin will hear us!

MISS

No, I will not leave it in strangers’ hands! Kill it instead, then!

JEAN

Bring the wretched creature here, then, and I shall wring its neck!

MISS

Yes, but do not hurt it! Do not—no, I cannot!

JEAN

Bring it here; I can!

MISS

takes the bird out of the cage and kisses it.

Oh, my little Serine, are you to die and leave your mistress now?

JEAN

Please do not make a scene; it is your life, your welfare, that is at stake! Come, quickly!

Snatches the bird from her; carries it to the chopping block and takes the kitchen axe.

Miss turns away.

JEAN

You should have learned to slaughter chickens instead of shooting a revolver—

strikes

Then you would not have fainted at a drop of blood!

MISS

screams.

Kill me too! Kill me! You who can slaughter an innocent animal without your hand trembling. Oh, I hate and loathe you; there is blood between us! I curse the hour when I saw you, I curse the hour when I was born in my mother’s womb!

JEAN

Yes, what good does it do for you to curse! Go!

MISS

approaches the chopping block as though drawn there against her will.

No, I do not want to go yet; I cannot—I must see—quiet! There is a carriage driving outside—

Listens toward the outside, all the while keeping her eyes fixed on the block and the axe.

Do you think I cannot look at blood! Do you think I am so weak—oh—I should like to see your blood, your brain on a wooden block—I should like to see your whole sex swimming in a lake like that—I think I could drink from your skull, I should like to bathe my feet in your chest and I could eat your heart roasted whole!—You think I am weak; you think I love you because the fruit of my womb desired your seed; you think I want to carry your offspring beneath my heart and nourish it with my blood—bear your child and take your name—do you hear, what is your name?—I have never heard your surname—you probably have none, I suppose. I should become Mrs. “Gatehouse”—or Madam Dunghill—you dog who wears my collar, you farmhand who wears my owner’s mark on your buttons—I, share with my cook, rival my maid—oh! oh! oh!—You think I am cowardly and want to flee! No, now I shall stay—and let the thunder roll! My father comes home—finds his escritoire broken open—his money gone—then he rings—that bell—twice for the valet—and then he sends for the sheriff—and then I tell everything! Everything! Oh, it will be good to have an end—if only it would end—and then he has a stroke and dies!—then we shall all be finished—and then there will be calm—peace—eternal rest—and then the coat of arms is shattered against the coffin—the count’s line is extinguished and the valet’s line continues in a foundling home—wins its laurels in a gutter and ends in a prison!

JEAN

Now it is the royal blood speaking! Good, Miss Julie! Just put the miller in the sack too!

Kristin enters, dressed for church, with a hymnbook in her hand.

MISS

Hurries toward her and falls into her arms as though seeking protection.

Help me, Kristin! Help me against this man!

KRISTIN

motionless and cold.

What sort of spectacle is this on a holy-day morning!

Looks at the chopping block.

And how you have fouled things up here!—What is the meaning of this? And all this screaming and noise!

MISS

Kristin! You are a woman and you are my friend! Beware of this scoundrel!

JEAN

abashed.

While the ladies discuss matters, I shall go in and shave!

Slips out to the right.

MISS

You must understand me; and you must listen to me!

KRISTIN

No, I really do not understand this sort of sluttishness! Where is Miss going, dressed for travel like this—and he is standing there with his hat on—eh?—eh?—

MISS

Hear me, Kristin; listen to me, and I shall tell you everything—

KRISTIN

I do not want to know anything—

MISS

You must hear me—

KRISTIN

What is it about? Is it about the foolishness with Jean! Well, you see, I do not care about that at all! For I do not meddle in it. But if Miss means to trick him into running away, we shall put a stop to that!

MISS

extremely nervous.

Try now to remain calm, Kristin, and listen to me! I cannot stay here and Jean cannot stay here—we must therefore leave...

KRISTIN

Hm, hm!

MISS

brightening.

But you see, I have just had an idea—what if all three of us were to go—abroad—to Switzerland and set up a hotel together—I have money, you see—and Jean and I would run the whole thing—and you, I had thought, would take care of the kitchen—would that not be good!—Say yes now! And come with us, and then everything is arranged!—Say yes! Do!

Embraces Kristin and pats her.

KRISTIN

cold and thoughtful.

Hm, hm!

MISS

presto tempo.

You have never been away traveling, Kristin—you must go out and see the world—you cannot imagine how amusing it is to travel by train—new people incessantly—new countries—and then we shall come to Hamburg and see the Zoological Garden in passing—you will like that—and then we shall go to the theater and listen to opera.—And when we come to Munich, we have the museums—you—and there are Rubens and Raphael, those great painters, as you know—you have heard of Munich, where King Ludwig lived—the king, I mean—who went mad—and then we shall see his castles—he still has castles that are furnished exactly as in fairy tales—and from there it is not far to Switzerland—with the Alps, you know—just think, the Alps with snow on them in the middle of summer—and there oranges and laurels grow and remain green all year round—
